title: SC: Palmetto and The Giant Conspiracy
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene dissects a South Carolina think-tank report that catalogues teachers unions, school boards, associations, accreditors and others as a left-wing conspiracy against the state's schools. He traces the funders and personnel behind the report, notes that its leader is about to take charge of state education, and walks through its sections pointing out exaggeration and guilt by association. His broader claim is that such reports are not meant to persuade but to give culture-war ranters an official-looking document to cite, in service of school-choice policy. It is school-policy commentary rather than classroom craft, so it sits closest to Practice and Culture, in line with how the archive treats his policy writing.
points: The report follows a familiar playbook of loudly stating a problem, proposing a solution, and never showing the solution will fix it.
Greene argues the choice movement uses culture-war framing to push choice policies, with ideologues stirred up by opportunists for hire.
The dossier treats ordinary union activity, including pay demands and strikes as bargaining leverage, as evidence of socialist intent.
Its function is to supply slickly produced, official-looking ammunition for those who want to say they are not just ranting.
The author warns that the head of the organization behind the report will soon run education in South Carolina, which bodes badly for teachers.
quotes: The basic thesis here is a version of what Butcher's old mentor Jay Greene laid out in February-- choicers need to use the culture wars to help push choice policies.

Butcher wants you to know that the Nation's Report Card shows steep declines in learning, yet while some states have instituted education savings accounts (ESAs), South Carolina has not. Also, a bicycle, because a vest has no sleeves. This is a classic trick--state in loud tones the problem, propose your solution, and never provide evidence that your solution will actually solve the problem.

So, two take-aways here-- the leftists are a minority, and everyone who isn't openly with the right is, either by inclination or intimidation, against them. I half-expect, "When we crush the unions and socialists, we will be greeted as liberators.
Nobody "favors" strikes and walkouts. Nobody. "Never mind sitting down to work this out at the bargaining table--I just want to go on strike," said no union member ever.

Is there anybody on any side of any issue who doesn't go out to recruit litigants? I do wish there was further explanation of the difference between "extreme" and "mild" views of the separation between church and state.

Diversity is okay, but only the right kind. I'm hearing echoes of every person who ever complained that Civil Rights activists had a point, but they were going about it all wrong and would they please just shut up and wait.

The report's function is not to rant and rave. Reports like this (all the way back to A Nation at Risk) provide ammunition to the ranters and ravers, allowing them to hold up the slickly produced official-looking pages and say, "I'm not just ranting and raving--what I have to say is supported by this sober academic report.
